LOWE FOR PRIME MINISTER? NOW LOOK BEHIND THE HEADLINE.

By Steve English · 25 October 2026

A poll puts Rupert Lowe ahead of Nigel Farage—for Prime Minister.

(Britain has no such head-to-head public vote. Nobody wins Downing Street by winning this question. Now look at the facts behind the headline.)

More in Common’s survey gives Lowe a 52–48 advantage over Farage when respondents must choose between them.

Sounds impressive.

But respondents were told to pick someone even if they disliked both. They were not choosing a party, a manifesto or a candidate in their constituency.

So what happens when people are asked which party they actually intend to vote for?

Reform 22%. Restore 3%.

Those are the figures from YouGov’s 18–19 October voting-intention poll.

More than seven times as much support for Reform.

The hypothetical Prime Minister contest puts Lowe narrowly ahead. The party-voting question puts Restore miles behind.

That is the difference between being someone’s preferred alternative to Nigel Farage and building a party they intend to elect.

Look at who put Lowe ahead

More in Common’s own tables reveal something the headline alone cannot tell you.

Among people who voted Conservative in 2024, Farage beats Lowe 63–37.

Among 2024 Reform voters, Farage wins 72–28.

The preference reverses among people who voted Labour, Liberal Democrat or Green.

Preferred Prime Minister: Farage or Lowe?
Party voted for in 2024FarageLowe
Conservative63%37%
Reform UK72%28%
Labour44%56%
Liberal Democrat44%56%
Green26%74%

Rounded figures; these groups describe respondents’ 2024 votes. Source: More in Common, 16–19 October 2026.

Lowe’s overall advantage therefore sits alongside Farage winning comfortably among both former Conservative and Reform voters.

My reading is straightforward: some of those choosing Lowe are registering their opposition to Farage, rather than their support for Restore.

If you vote Labour and consider Reform a serious electoral threat, choosing its much smaller rival is hardly a political conversion.

“I would rather have him than Farage” does not mean “I will vote for his party.”

The survey records the choice, not the motive. But treating every reluctant preference as an endorsement would be absurd.

Now compare the actual parties

Here is the political organisation behind each man.

The elected footprint
RepresentationReform UKRestore Britain
MPs81
Council seats held directly2,29629
Councils with representatives23017
Councils under outright majority control230
Councils led, including minority administrations350

Listings checked on 25 October 2026. Seat and council-presence totals are calculated from the individual party rosters. Restore’s Great Yarmouth First affiliate holds another nine separately listed council seats. Councils led includes those under outright majority control. Sources: UK Parliament, Open Council Data and council composition listings.

Reform has thousands of council seats and leads dozens of councils. Restore has a small scattering of representatives and leads none.

Not even Great Yarmouth Borough Council, in Lowe’s own parliamentary constituency.

That is the gulf a personal-preference headline can conceal.

Restore can attract attention and compete for votes. But a forced-choice question cannot turn its present organisation into something remotely comparable with Reform’s.

A tadpole does not become a whale because it wins a hypothetical swimming contest.

And about those “cast-offs”…

Reform’s opponents like to dismiss it as a collection of former Conservatives.

Then look inside Restore.

Twenty-six of its 29 directly affiliated councillors came from Reform UK.

Add Rupert Lowe, its sole MP, who was himself elected under the Reform banner.

That makes 27 of its 30 directly affiliated councillors and MPs—exactly 90%—former Reform representatives.

So if former party membership is the test, what exactly is Restore supposed to be?

Reform Mk II?

Apparently, changing parties makes you a cast-off when you join Reform, but a principled patriot when you leave it.

How convenient.

The argument collapses under its own double standard. Restore cannot sensibly be presented as a clean break from Reform while relying so heavily on people who previously represented it.

The headline and the reality

“Lowe beats Farage for Prime Minister” makes an excellent headline for Rupert Lowe.

But look beyond it.

In YouGov’s party poll, Restore stands at 3% against Reform’s 22%. Its directly affiliated elected ranks consist of one MP and 29 councillors. It leads no councils. And 90% of those representatives previously represented Reform.

Those facts belong alongside the 52–48 headline.

Being preferred to Nigel Farage when voters are denied every other option is one thing. Persuading them to elect your party is another.

Steve English | 25 October 2026
